drills.coachNote: White's rook on b6 is ready to swing to b8 with check, and the pawn on d6 already eyes your knight on e7 — more than one threat is brewing. Kd8 walked into the worst version of it: Rb8+ forced Nc8, tangling knight and king on the back rank, then c6 and Rh7 tore into your rook and pawns — a brutal 7.9-pawn swing. Kc8 sidesteps the check entirely, keeping your knight and rook independent; White still grinds on with c6, Bc4, dxe7, Kc7, Rb7+ and does win the knight eventually, but your pieces stay coordinated instead of collapsing on one square. Pick the king square that avoids checks which box in your other pieces.

drills.coachNote: White's king on g1 is boxed in by his own rook on h1, and your rook on f2 already covers the f-file, leaving him nowhere to run from a check on g2. drills.coachNote: Black's king on e7 has one job here — stay central so it can react to whichever side you push your pawns, which means the square your own king takes right now decides how cleanly you finish. Kf4 still wins, but it lets Black shuffle back with Kf7 and hang around a little longer, which is why the evaluation drops by over ten pawns even though the position stays won. Kf3 does the same job while staying better placed to support your queenside pawns, and after Kf3 Kf7 e4 Ke7 Ke3 your king marches through the center on the most direct route. With this much material banked, precision is about not handing your opponent extra moves to make trouble.

Ba2 clears that square first, so after Ba2 Ke7 Kc4 Ke8 Kb5 your king marches straight at the queenside pawns while Black's king is stuck shuffling between e8 and d8. drills.coachNote: Black's queen on g5 and rook on f2 are both bearing down on your knight on d2, which sits one square from your own king on e1 and is the only thing keeping that square safe. drills.title: vs debaser7 (798) — Slav Defense
drills.coachNote: White's plan is simple — push the a6 and b6 pawns toward queening, and every tempo he saves along the way matters since your rook is the only thing stopping them. Rc4+ feels active, but it's a check that costs White nothing: he just answers Kd5, marching his king forward to help the pawns, and after Rc3 b7 Rb3 the pawn is a rank closer to queening than it needed to be, which is why your big edge shrinks. Rc1 instead gets your rook behind the pawns on the file they're heading toward, so when White pushes b7 you have Re1+ to harass the king and Rb1 to sit right behind the pawn, as in Rc1 b7 Re1+ Kd5 Rb1 Rc6. Against advanced connected pawns, put your rook behind them, don't spend checks that only speed up your opponent's king.

Your rook on c7 gives that up: after b6 your rook is on the wrong side, Rc1 comes too late, b7 forces Ra1, and the pawns run — a completely winning endgame at -6.5 turns into a real fight. Ra7 was the move, staying on the a-file behind both pawns; after Re8 Kh5 Kd6 Kg5 Rg8+ your king mops up while the rook holds the blockade. Against connected passers, put your rook behind them on the file, not off to the side.

drills.coachNote: You've spotted that Black's back rank is weak with the king jammed between rooks on e8 and g8, and you want to cash in with a capture-check. The g8 rook only looks free — grabbing it with Qxg8+ lets Black simply reply Kxg8, since nothing on the g-file punishes the king for taking, so you've handed over your queen for a single rook. Two rooks for a queen after Rxe8+ Kf7 Re3 doesn't come close to your +4.6 edge. The e8 rook was the one to take: Kxe8 runs straight into Re1+, so Black must dodge with ...Kg7, and Qd7+ Kh8 Re8 lets you walk off with a full rook for free. When two pieces look equally hanging, check which capture is actually defended before committing.
drills.threat: Black's king on f8 is wedged between two rooks on e8 and g8, but only one of those captures is actually safe.

drills.coachNote: Right before this move, White's knight on g5 was simply hanging — nothing on the board defended it, and your pawn on h6 could grab it for free. Instead you played Qf5, sliding your queen off the seventh rank without touching the knight, and that gave White time to consolidate: the knight swings into the game with Ne4, hitting your queen for a tempo, and after ...Qg6 f3 Raa8 the position settles back to roughly balanced instead of you being a clean piece up. The move was hxg5 — just capturing the knight — after which h3 Qf5 a3 f6 f3 leaves you comfortably up material with no real compensation for White. Whenever a piece sits with nothing covering it, that's free material — grab it before looking for anything fancier.
drills.threat: White's knight on g5 has no defender right now — nothing covers that square at all.

drills.coachNote: That pawn on e6 looks like a free grab, but White's queen on e2 sits right behind it on the open e-file, and behind the queen a rook waits on e1 — the file is stacked two deep. Taking with Bxe6 walks straight into Qxe6+, and after your queen recaptures on e6 the rook is still there to swoop in with Rxe6, so you trade your bishop and queen for White's queen and a pawn, turning your -2.8 into something much worse. Re8 was the idea: adding your own rook to the file first forces the queen away with Qd1, and now Rxe6 wins the pawn cleanly, with Rxe6 Qxe6 leaving you simply a pawn up. Before grabbing something on an open file, count how many attackers and defenders are actually lined up behind it.

drills.coachNote: Black's queen on g5 already had its sights on g2 — that pawn was undefended, and because your rook sits on h1 right behind it, taking g2 comes with an attack on the rook too. Bf1 was the move, because the bishop on f1 directly covers g2, removing the capture entirely and letting you continue with c4, Nc3 and normal development. When a piece points straight down a file or diagonal at one of your pawns, check who's actually guarding it before pushing something else.
